messages.author: 9cf2f6f9b80e73cd
messages.subject: Correlation matrix in R
parts:
Hi,

I am very new to the R package and lavaan and I am currently teaching myself the programme. 
I understand that before I can specify my model, I need to do a correlation or a covariance matrix out of my data. 
I did just that but now I am confused on how do I enter this onto the R. The book says that I need to use "lower2full()" command.
However, my matrix has 37 columns and 37 rows, and I am not sure how to select the lower diagonal?
Sorry if this is a dumb question.

Vik

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: RE: Correlation matrix in R
parts:
Vik—

     You can enter the data itself, rather than a correlation or covariance matrix.  Doing this will give you better options.  R is designed for statistical analysis, so there are many ways to read data in.  One of the easiest methods is the read.clipboard function in the package “psych”.

     Open your data file, and copy the data, with variables names across the top.

     Then in R, load the psych package (if you have already installed it), and put your data into a data.frame:

 

library(psych)

mydata <- read.clipboard()

 

     If you have not yet installed the psych package, you will need to do that first.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Correlation matrix in R
parts:
On 03/23/2015 05:37 PM, vikg wrote:
> I understand that before I can specify my model, I need to do a
> correlation or a covariance matrix out of my data.

No need. You provide the full data (and if needed, lavaan will compute
the covariance matrix for you).

> I did just that but now I am confused on how do I enter this onto the R.
> The book says that I need to use "lower2full()" command.

I do not know which book you are referring to, but if you must use a
covariance matrix (instead of the full data) as input, and you already
have a full covariance matrix, you can use the sample.cov= argument (and
the sample.nobs= argument) of the regular sem/cfa fitting functions.

If you only have the lower triangular of the covariance matrix, you
could use the lower2full() function. But a much more convenient way is
to use the getCov() function in this case. See the help file for
getCov() to see some examples.

Yves.

parts:
Yes, it is as follows:

mydata<- read.csv("heis.csv")

myvars <- c("diagnosis","Gender","Speedprocess","Attentionvigil","Workingmem","Verballearn","Visuallearn","Reasonproblem","Socialcog","P1","P2","P3","P4","P5","P6","P7","N1","N2","N3","N4","N5","N6","N7","G1","G2","G3","G4","G5","G6","G7","G8","G9","G10","G11","G12","G13","G14","G15","G16")
newdata <- mydata[myvars]
newdata


#subset 1
newdata1<-subset(newdata,diagnosis== "1" )
#subset 2
newdata2<-subset(newdata,diagnosis== "2" )
#rbind together 
newdata3<-rbind(newdata1,newdata2)

newdata4<-subset(newdata,diagnosis>=1&diagnosis<3)
newdata5<-subset(newdata,Gender=="Female")

rownames(newdata5) <- NULL

newdata5

newdata.model<-'
cognition=~Speedprocess+Attentionvigil+Workingmem+Verballearn+Visuallearn+Reasonproblem+Socialcog
Panssp=~P1+P2+P3+P4+P5+P6+P7
Panssn=~N1+N2+N3+N4+N5+N6+N7
Panssg=~G1+G2+G3+G4+G5+G6+G7+G8+G9+G10+G11+G12+G13+G14+G15+G16
Cognition~Panssp
Cognition~Panssn
Cognition~Panssg
Panssp~Panssn
Panssp~Panssg
Panssn~Panssg'

sem.fit<-sem(newdata.model,data=newdata5)
summary(sem.fit,standardized=TRUE,fit.measures=TRUE)

On Mon, Mar 23, 2015 at 5:51 PM, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

Vik—

     You can enter the data itself, rather than a correlation or covariance matrix.  Doing this will give you better options.  R is designed for statistical analysis, so there are many ways to read data in.  One of the easiest methods is the read.clipboard function in the package “psych”.

     Open your data file, and copy the data, with variables names across the top.

     Then in R, load the psych package (if you have already installed it), and put your data into a data.frame:

 

library(psych)

mydata <- read.clipboard()

 

     If you have not yet installed the psych package, you will need to do that first.

--Ed Rigdon
